title: Global Companies Are Using India's IPO Market as an Exit Door. The Rupee Is Paying the Price.
excerpt: From Hyundai to Walmart's PhonePe, foreign firms are listing in India not to raise capital but to cash out — and the $23 billion in outflows this year shows the cost.
body:
India's booming IPO market has become the world's most efficient machine for extracting foreign profits from an emerging economy. A Reuters investigation published Thursday reveals the scale of the problem: global companies are listing their Indian subsidiaries not to raise capital for growth, but to sell existing shares and repatriate the proceeds back to their home countries.

The structure is called an Offer for Sale, and it has become the dominant format for major Indian IPOs. When Hyundai Motor listed its Indian unit in 2024 in the country's largest-ever IPO, not a single rupee of the proceeds went into expanding the business. The entire offering was an OFS — the Korean parent selling a portion of its stake to Indian retail and institutional investors.

LG Electronics is doing the same. So is PhonePe, Walmart's Indian payments unit. Carlsberg is planning an Indian IPO that will also be entirely OFS, according to banking sources. The Danish brewer confirmed it is "exploring different options for increasing shareholder value which may potentially include an Indian IPO."

The Numbers Behind the Drain

Between 2021 and 2025, Indian IPOs raised ₹5.4 lakh crore — roughly $60 billion. Of that, ₹3.37 lakh crore, or 66 per cent, came through OFS exits by promoters, early investors, and foreign parents. Only ₹2.03 lakh crore was fresh capital raised for business operations.

The pattern has accelerated. In 2026, foreign portfolio investors have sold more than $23 billion of Indian equity holdings, smashing 2025's record outflows of $18.9 billion. The IPO-linked repatriations are layered on top of this already devastating tide.

MUFG Bank, in a January analysis, concluded that "one important contributor to Indian rupee weakness has been the strong IPO market in India." Tanay Dalal, a senior vice president at Axis Bank, put it more precisely: IPO-linked capital outflows are "exerting a steady, though not abrupt, depreciation bias on the rupee."

The rupee has fallen 13 per cent against the dollar since 2024 and six per cent so far in 2026 — its worst annual performance in nearly a decade.

Why Companies Are Choosing India as an Exit

The motive is simple arithmetic. Indian stock markets have carried sky-high valuations for several years, driven by a massive domestic retail investor base that has poured savings into equities through systematic investment plans. The average P/E ratio for OFS-structured IPOs over the past five years has been 57 times earnings — compared to the Nifty 50's historical range of 20 to 30 times.

For a foreign parent sitting on a stake in an Indian subsidiary, those valuations create an opportunity that does not exist in most other markets. A company can sell a minority stake at 50 or 60 times earnings, repatriate the dollars, and still retain controlling ownership.

"India listings provide them liquidity as well as a positive impact on the market cap for their parent," said Prashant Gupta, a partner at law firm Shardul Amarchand, which advised Hyundai and LG on their IPOs.

What It Means for Indian Investors and the Diaspora

For India's 100 million-plus retail investors who have entered the stock market through SIPs and mutual funds in recent years, the OFS trend poses a structural concern. They are buying shares at elevated valuations from sellers who are explicitly cashing out — not from companies investing in future growth.

An analysis by The Hindu Business Line found that 68 fully OFS IPOs over the past five years had collectively lost ₹95,000 crore from their listing-day market capitalisation. More than 61 per cent of them now trade below their listing price.

For NRI investors, the dynamic is particularly ironic. Money that members of the diaspora invest in India through mutual funds or direct equity purchases may be funding the exit of a Korean automaker or a European consumer goods company, with the proceeds heading out of the country and weakening the very currency their NRE deposits are denominated in.

India's Chief Economic Advisor V. Anantha Nageswaran warned in November that IPOs had "increasingly become exit vehicles for early investors rather than mechanisms for raising long-term capital." He added: "This undermines the spirit of public markets."

The government has not indicated any plans to curb the OFS trend. But on the same day this analysis was published, the cabinet approved the scrapping of capital gains tax on foreign investment in government bonds — an acknowledgement that the outflow problem has grown serious enough to demand emergency action on other fronts.
